title: Tools
text:
I’ve made open-source tools about local communities and their needs for NHS Public Health staff.
Poverty and emergency hospital admissions
Overcrowding and vaccine needs
Funding in priority neighbourhoods

title: Analysis & Policy
text:
Housing and Health
We found that council tenants are much more likely to have respiratory, cardiovascular, and mental health conditions, including people living in homes that failed energy efficiency standards. We are now developing a project to prioritise these homes for repair.


Who Waits Longest?
Read our briefing paper that describes inequalities in waiting times for hospital treatments – people who live in the most deprived areas wait longer for treatment and people from Black or Asian ethnic backgrounds tended to wait longer than white patients.


Losing Preventative Care
We analysed patient pathways into and out of hospitals and found that pre-COVID, community medical centres were used primarily for preventative care, but they are now mostly used for patients’ recovery after a hospitalisation.


Children’s Mental Health Inequalities
We showed that use of mental health medication has increased steeply, and younger children and boys are more likely to be rejected by mental health services. We also found that children deemed at significant risk of harm by social workers used five times more mental healthcare.


Coronavirus
During the pandemic, I led a Chief Scientist’s Office project to protect patients with serious medical conditions from coronavirus.
We advised the NHS on how to protect these patients as they receive necessary care during the pandemic.


Data Provenance
I ran Wellcome Trust Open Research project to design safe ways to be open while using high-security patient data. We automated the capture and reporting of complex data provenance without compromising patient data privacy.


Research Culture
Scientists should be (but aren’t!) rewarded for doing rigorous science.
I gave evidence about this to the House of Commons Science & Technology committee.
You can watch a symposium I hosted: Academic Journals are Broken. Let’s Build a Better Scientific Record.

title: Publications page update: summary
text:
Workspace: C:\Users\computer\Documents\JessButler.github.io, a Quarto website for Jessica E. Butler (Lead Data Scientist at NHS Grampian and Senior Research Fellow at the University of Aberdeen). Key files are index.qmd, publications.qmd, research.qmd and talks.qmd, plus posts under posts/. ORCID: 0000-0003-2054-3777. Google Scholar: https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=N3iK7TcAAAAJ
Request: find publications by this author that were missing from the site’s publications page, search the web thoroughly, find DOIs, search for conference abstracts, and update publications.qmd. Each entry should have a source link and DOI, and each conference abstract should be listed once alongside its full paper.




Original page. publications.qmd held only five items, all from 2021-2022: the CYP mental health briefing, the BMC Psychiatry 2023 paper, the CEV briefing, the medRxiv shielding preprint, and two Health Foundation blog posts.
Source gathering. I compared the Scholar profile, ORCID (24 works, nothing after 2023), Crossref, PMC, Health Foundation pages and the Aberdeen research portal.

The Health Foundation site and the Aberdeen portal returned HTTP 403 on direct fetches.
Crossref intermittently returned HTTP 429.
Europe PMC returned nothing for her ORCID.
Of the 38 pages of the ACHDS publications list, I checked only pages 1-7, and found only the Scheliga 2026 entry.

Rewrite. I wrote a new publications.qmd with these sections:

Networked Data Lab and linked data
Children’s mental health
Coronavirus
Open science and reproducibility
Multimorbidity and cohort studies
Mental health services
Earlier work in microbial genomics

Layout. Each entry has an author/year/title link, journal, and DOI where one exists. Conference abstracts and preprints are nested as sub-bullets under their full papers.
Confirmed DOIs.

IJPDS 2026: 10.23889/ijpds.v11i5.3600 (Butler & Knight), v11i5.3736 (elective care) and v11i5.3680 (Scheliga). The Scheliga paper also has an Aberdeen repository DOI, 10.20392/CK8D-YC88.
Social Science & Medicine 2024: 10.1016/j.socscimed.2024.117057. Its SSM abstract is 10.1136/jech-2024-ssmabstracts.2, and its preprint is 10.1101/2023.10.13.23296488.
Health Foundation: 10.37829/HF-2024-NDL01 (intermediate care), 10.37829/hf-2022-ndl1 (CYP briefing) and 10.37829/HF-2021-NDL01 (CEV briefing).
IJPDS 7(3) abstracts: 1897 (shielding), 1909 (provenance), 1912 (public involvement), and 1980 (children’s mental health).
Lancet Infect Dis RECOVERY sotrovimab: 10.1016/S1473-3099(25)00361-5.
Journal of Neuroscience Methods UKRN paper: 10.1016/j.jneumeth.2023.109949.
The remaining DOIs came from her ORCID record.

Better Homes briefing. I confirmed from the Health Foundation page that “Jessica E Butler” is a listed author of Better homes, better health: insights from linking housing and health data (May 2026). I added it to the Networked Data Lab section as “Butler JE, et al. (2026)”. The page showed no full author list and I found no DOI.
2025 provenance paper. I checked Semi-automated data provenance tracking… (IJPDS 10(2), DOI 10.23889/ijpds.v10i2.2464) in Crossref. The authors are O’Sullivan, Markovic, Dymiter, Scheliga, Odo and Wilde. Butler is not an author, so I left it out.





No DOI found: the 2025 Health Foundation elective care briefing, the Better Homes briefing, and the Ball et al. 2025 OP21 abstract (J Epidemiol Community Health 79 Suppl 1, A10-A11). Crossref was rate-limited when I tried the OP21 abstract. The two Health Foundation blog posts have no DOI.
Inferred and unverified: the 1980 abstract DOI is inferred from its article number, and the ijpds.org source links for 1909 and 1980 follow the site’s URL pattern without being opened. The 2022 IJPDS items are labelled “IPDLN conference abstracts” based on volume and numbering, not the conference programme. The author lists of several entries are truncated with “et al.” from Scholar.
Deliberately left out:

The Mahadevan 2006 and Geobacter review papers.
Hurricane sediment papers, the 1986 Fermilab report, and duplicate Scholar entries.
The 2016 Wood et al. poster, which is peer-reviewed but has no DOI.
The ICIC25 integrated care abstract from Prendergast (International Journal of Integrated Care, DOI 10.5334/ijic.ICIC25388), because I haven’t confirmed Butler is an author.

Not yet done: I haven’t rendered the Quarto site to check the page displays correctly. publications.qmd is the only file changed.

title: Mental health medication for children
text:
We looked at all children living in the NHS Grampian region (Aberdeen City, Aberdeenshire and Moray). There were 100,000 people under age 18 in total.
We measured how many prescriptions these children had for mental health medicine. This included medicine for ADHD, anxiety, depression, sleep problems, and psychoses.
We asked these questions

What kind of medicine for mental health do children take?
Are they taking more of these medicines than before?
Are boys and girls given different medicine?
Are younger children given different medicine than older children?

What did we find?


Prescriptions to children up 60%
3% of all children had a prescription for mental health medicine in 2021.
Since 2015, the number of prescriptions has risen from 24,000 to 37,000 per year.

Sleep prescriptions are up 91%
Antidepressant prescriptions are up 59%
ADHD prescriptions are up 45%
Anti-psychotic prescriptions are up 35%




Boys get far more prescriptions than girls
Boys get 70% of all prescriptions for mental health medicine. This difference is largest in the youngest children. Boys get the vast majority of prescriptions given to primary schoolers. Girls’ prescriptions increase rapidly after age 13.




Young children take ADHD medication & older children take anti-depressants
We looked at the kinds of medicine given to children of different ages.
Primary schoolers take mostly ADHD and sleep medication. By the end of secondary school, many more take anti-depressants.
Comparing boys and girls shows that boys are given mental health medicine at younger ages, mostly for ADHD and sleep.
Girls get many more prescriptions after puberty, mostly for anti-depressants.




Children living in poverty take much more mental health medicine
We compared children living in the poorest areas to those living in the wealthiest areas. Children living in poor neighbourhoods had twice as many prescriptions for mental health problems.
For every 100 children living in the poorest areas, there were 34 mental health prescriptions every year. In the wealthiest areas there were 17 prescriptions.



Tell me more
This research was done as part of the Networked Data Lab with partners at The Health Foundation.
William Ball led this analysis with me. Other contributors from the Aberdeen Centre for Health Data Science were: Corri Black, Sharon Gordon, Bārbala Ostrovska, Shantini Paranjothy, Adelene Rasalam, David Ritchie, Helen Rowlands, Elaine Thompson, Magdalena Rzewuska, and Katie Wilde.
Full details are in our publication Inequalities in children’s mental health care: analysis of routinely collected data on prescribing and referrals to secondary care.
Policy recommendations from our work are in the briefing Improving children and young people’s mental health services

title: Goldacre Report
section: Better, broader, safer: using health data for research and analysis
text:
Better, broader, safer: using health data for research and analysis
The Goldacre review was tasked with finding ways to deliver better, broader, safer use of NHS data for analysis and research.
The recommendations are derived from extensive engagement with over 300 individuals, 8 focus groups, 100 written submissions, substantial desk research, and detailed discussion with our senior stakeholder group.

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Report topic areas

Security
Modern methods
Data curation
Data analysts
Governance
Strategy

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Security

All NHS policies should acknowledge the shortcomings of ‘pseudonymisation’ for managing patient privacy
Build a small number of secure analytics platforms (Trusted Research Environments)
Shut down all flows of psudonymised GP data as soon as TREs are built

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Security

Create faster data access rules and processes for safe users
Use TREs for all analysis of NHS patient records by NHS staff, academics and innovators
Publish logs of all TRE activity

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Modern methods

Reproducible Analytical Pathways should be the minimum standard for all NHS data analysis
All code for NHS data curation and analysis should be shared openly
Fund competitive, high status, standalone software projects and developers

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Data curation

Stop doing data curation differently and duplicatively in every team and project
Recognise NHS data curation as a complex, high status technical challenge
Devote teams to systematic curation work, using shared practices, code, tools, and documentation
Create an open online library for NHS data curation code, validity tests, and technical documentation

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Data analysts careers

Create an NHS Analyst Service modelled on the Government Economic Service and Statistical Service
NHS Analyst Service should have:

a head of profession

clear job descriptions tied to technical skills

progression opportunities to become a senior analyst

realistic salaries for expensive specific skills

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Data analysis training

Create an Open College for NHS Analysts
The Open College should provide initial training and continuing professional development tied to job descriptions
All Open College content should be shared openly online
Train senior non-analysts and leaders to be good customers of data teams

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Governance

End trusts and GPs all acting as separate data controllers
Create a single application for all ethics, governance, and access permissions
Publish access delays annually

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Governance

Get appropriate financial return where marketable innovations are driven by NHS data
Avoid exclusive commercial arrangements
Disclose all funding for TREs including: source, amount, recipients, objectives, and outputs

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Strategy

Rapidly create Data Pioneer Groups to develop open methods, code, and technical documentation
Data Pioneer Groups should initially be separate from ‘business as usual’, but should incrementally subsume it

title: Goldacre Report
text:
Strategy

Create very senior strategic leadership roles for developers, data architects and data scientists
Develop a common TRE service run by civil servants

title: Blogs
text:
Goldacre Report


Improving research and analysis with NHS data


A summary of the Goldacre review’s recommendations for making NHS data safer and more useful for research and analysis.















From preventing hospital admissions to recovering from them


Evolution of community care in Grampian


Community care centres in Grampian have shifted from GP-led preventative care to long-stay recovery for older, sicker patients leaving hospital.















Mental health medication for children





Prescriptions for mental health medicine to children in NHS Grampian rose 60% since 2015. Boys receive most, and children in poorer areas receive twice as many.















Children’s specialist mental health care





Referrals of teenagers to specialist mental health services are rising, but rejections of young children are up too. Boys are now treated half as often as girls.

title: From preventing hospital admissions to recovering from them
text:
Summary
Our key finding is that since 2019, NHS Grampian’s community care settings changed from providing short-term, preventative care, to providing long-term post-acute care.
Key policy questions follow:
Are these care centres the right settings for step-down and end-of-life care? If so, where should the lost preventative and scheduled care take place?
We note that in order to proactively plan a balance of preventative and acute care, more data sharing is required. Though intermediate care is delivered by Health and Social Care Partnerships in Scotland, patient data are not shared between the primary and secondary care, nor with social care. No true integrated care can take place until data for the entire patient journey can be linked.

Tell me more
This research was done as part of the Networked Data Lab with partners at The Health Foundation.
Frank Popham led this analysis with me. Other contributors were: Corri Black, Corri Black, Raul Berrocal-Martin, Sharon Gordon, Kate O’Sullivan, Helen Rowlands, Bernhard Scheliga, Irmina Zborowska, and the NHS Grampian Public Health – Health Intelligence Team.
Policy recommendations from our work are in the briefing Are intermediate care services stretched too thin?. Please see the appendices therein for more details.

title: Children’s specialist mental health care
text:
We looked at all children living in the NHS Grampian region (Aberdeen City, Aberdeenshire and Moray). There were 100,000 people under age 18 in total.
We studied children’s referrals to see specialist doctors in out-patient clinics.
We asked these questions

How many children are referred to mental health specialists?
Are more being referred than before?
Which children are accepted for specialist treatment?
Are boys and girls treated differently?
Are older and younger children treated differently?

What did we find?


Many children need specialist mental health care
3% of all children were referred to see a mental health specialist in 2020.



Older children’s mental healthcare needs are rising
Teenagers are being referred to see mental health specialists more often. Referrals are up about 30% since 2015.
Referrals for primary school children have not risen. Referrals for children under 5 are down.




Mental health specialists treat mostly teenagers
We measured which children’s referrals for specialist care were rejected.
20% of secondary schooler’s referrals for mental healthcare are rejected. This hasn’t changed over time.
50% of referrals for young children are rejected. There has been is a large increase in rejection of young children since 2015.
The children treated in the specialist mental health clinics now average 1.5 years older than in 2015.




Boys are being treated less by mental health specialists
In 2015, mental health specialists treated equal numbers of girls and boys. Now boys are being referred less and rejected more. There are now twice as many girls being treated by specialists as boys.




Children living in poverty need more specialist care younger
We compared children living in the poorest areas to those living in the wealthiest areas. Children living in poor neighbourhoods had twice as many referrals for specialist mental health care.
The average age of a child’s first referral to specialist is over a year younger for those living in the most deprived areas.



Tell me more
This research was done as part of the Networked Data Lab with partners at The Health Foundation.
William Ball led this analysis with me. Other contributors from the Aberdeen Centre for Health Data Science were: Corri Black, Sharon Gordon, Bārbala Ostrovska, Shantini Paranjothy, Adelene Rasalam, David Ritchie, Helen Rowlands, Elaine Thompson, Magdalena Rzewuska, and Katie Wilde.
Full details are in our publication Inequalities in children’s mental health care: analysis of routinely collected data on prescribing and referrals to secondary care.
Policy recommendations from our work are in the briefing Improving children and young people’s mental health services
